title: "Yet Will I Trust in Him"
scripture:
Job 1:1–5 — Job was a man "perfect and upright, and one that feared God, and eschewed evil." He offered burnt offerings for his children continually, saying, "It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts."

Job 1:6–22 — The Adversary challenges Job's integrity. The Lord permits testing but preserves Job's life. Job loses livestock, servants, and all ten children in a single day. His response: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord."

Job 2 — Job is smitten with "sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown." His wife says, "Curse God, and die." Job replies, "Shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?"

Job 12–14 — Job's reply to his friends. "With the ancient is wisdom; and in length of days understanding" (12:12). Job desires to reason with God (13:3). "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble" (14:1).

Job 19:23–27 — Job's powerful testimony: "For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God."

Job 38–40 — The Lord answers out of the whirlwind. "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (38:4). God's wisdom and power displayed in creation.

Job 42 — Job's repentance: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee" (42:5). The Lord restores Job's fortunes, giving him twice as much as before.
commentary:
Key Themes

  • Integrity under pressure — Job's blamelessness wasn't transactional; it wasn't "good behavior for blessings." It was who he was.
  • The theology of the friends vs. Job's reality — Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar represent retribution theology (suffering = sin). Job knows this is false. The Lord ultimately condemns the friends (42:7).
  • The Redeemer testimony (19:25–27) — One of the clearest Old Testament witnesses of Christ's resurrection and our own. "In my flesh shall I see God" — physical resurrection.
  • God's answer: not explanations, but Himself — The whirlwind speeches (38–41) don't answer "why." They reveal Who. "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee" (42:5).

Scholarly Insights

BYU Studies (Old Testament, Lesson 33): Job's "legal metaphor" — he wants a daysman (mediator/umpire) between himself and God (9:33). Christ fulfills this.

followHIM Podcast (Dr. Marcus Martins): Job's daughters' names (Jemima, Kezia, Keren-happuch) — only the daughters are named in the restoration (42:14). Symbolic of beauty from ashes, restoration beyond the patriarchal norm.

Scripture Insights (Taylor Halverson): Psalms 1–2 as "trailer" for the Psalter; Job as wisdom literature's exploration of theodicy — not a theoretical problem, but a lived crisis.
application:
Personal Application

This Week: Identify one area where you've assumed "righteousness = protection from suffering." Surrender that transactional view. Trust God's character, not His calculator.

Action Items

  1. Read Job 19:23–27 aloud daily — Let the Redeemer testimony settle in your bones.
  2. Journal: When have you demanded "why" and received "Who" instead? Write about a time God answered your crisis with His presence, not an explanation.
  3. Pray for someone in the "ash heap" — Not for their suffering to end, but for them to see God in it (42:5).
  4. Memorize: "Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him" (Job 13:15).

Teaching Prompts (EQ)

  • Ask: "What's the difference between integrity and performance?"
  • Discuss: The friends spoke true principles (God is just) but misapplied them. How do we avoid this?
  • Testify: The Redeemer lives. Our resurrection is as certain as His.
